introduction-the-era-of-pets.core: Before cloud, servers were expensive, long-lived hardware, so you named them and maintained them for years. Configuration management tools (CFEngine, Puppet, Chef, Salt) emerged to keep those pets consistent by continuously enforcing desired state. Understanding why they were built that way explains both their strengths and why cloud-native patterns now often replace them.

first_principles.problem: A team inherits a 10-year-old Puppet codebase and wonders whether to keep it or replace it.

analogy.title: Maintaining a classic car fleet
analogy.story: You keep detailed service schedules because replacing a car is unthinkable; with rental fleets, you just swap cars.
analogy.breaks: Classic cars appreciate; old servers accumulate risk.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each wave reflects cheaper, more disposable compute.

check.q: Why did early CM tools enforce state continuously?
check.a: Servers lived for years and were changed by many people, so constant convergence was the only way to fight accumulating drift.

configuration-drift-the-core-problem-the.core: Configuration drift is the gradual divergence of servers from their intended state: emergency hotfixes, manual package installs, partial failures and differing patch levels. It leads to snowflake servers, 'works on server A but not B' bugs, and failed audits. CM tools fight drift by repeatedly converging to declared state; immutable infrastructure prevents it by never changing running servers.

first_principles.problem: A bug appears only on 3 of 20 identical web servers because someone hotfixed a library on them.
truths: Manual changes are inevitable under pressure.
Either converge often or never change.

analogy.title: A garden left untended
analogy.story: Weeds appear gradually; either weed weekly (converge) or lay fresh turf each season (replace).
analogy.breaks: Weeds are visible; drift hides until something breaks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows drift without fixing; a normal run would converge it.

check.q: What are the two strategies against configuration drift?
check.a: Continuously converge servers back to desired state (CM tools), or prevent drift by never modifying running servers (immutability).

the-masteragent-architecture.core: Puppet and Chef use a pull model. An agent on every node periodically (for example every 30 minutes) contacts a central server, sends facts about itself, receives a compiled catalog or run list, and enforces it locally. This scales to many thousands of nodes and gives continuous enforcement, but needs agents everywhere, PKI and certificates, a highly available server, and adds latency to urgent changes.

first_principles.problem: An urgent firewall change takes up to 30 minutes to reach all nodes, and the Puppet server is a single point of failure.

analogy.title: Branch offices calling HQ for instructions
analogy.story: Each office calls in on schedule, describes itself, and gets its tailored instructions.
analogy.breaks: Offices can be called urgently; agents wait for their interval unless triggered.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every node with this class converges every 30 min.

check.q: What does a Puppet agent send to the server before receiving its catalog?
check.a: Facts about the node (OS, IPs, hardware, custom facts) used to compile a tailored catalog.

agentless-vs-agent-based-the-ansible-dis.core: Ansible disrupted the market by being agentless: no daemon to install, no PKI, just SSH and Python already present on servers. Changes are pushed on demand rather than pulled on a schedule. That lowers adoption cost and suits ad-hoc orchestration, but there's no continuous enforcement unless you schedule runs (AWX/AAP), and push over SSH is slower at very large scale.

first_principles.problem: A team avoids configuration management because installing and certifying Puppet agents on every server is too much work.
truths: Push and pull have different timing.
derivation: Pick based on **fleet size and drift needs**.

analogy.title: A visiting technician vs an on-site employee
analogy.story: The technician comes when called, needing no desk; the employee is always there but needs a badge and an office.
analogy.breaks: Technicians can't fix things while away; schedule runs to compensate.

check.q: What do you lose by default when moving from Puppet to Ansible?
check.a: Continuous automatic enforcement; Ansible only converges when a run is triggered, so you must schedule runs.

saltstack-the-hybrid-approach.core: Salt combines models. Minions keep a persistent connection to the master over a ZeroMQ event bus, so commands reach thousands of nodes in seconds (push speed with agent scale). It also supports agentless salt-ssh, scheduled state enforcement, and an event-driven reactor that triggers states automatically on events, such as remediating when a beacon detects a changed file.

first_principles.problem: A team needs to run an emergency command across 10,000 servers in seconds and also auto-remediate drift.
truths: One tool can offer several models.

analogy.title: An office with a PA system and sensors
analogy.story: Announcements reach everyone instantly, and sensors trigger the cleaning crew automatically when something spills.
analogy.breaks: PA systems are one-way; Salt's bus returns results too.

check.q: What do Salt beacons and reactors enable?
check.a: Event-driven automation: beacons detect changes on minions and reactors trigger states in response, enabling auto-remediation.

migration-strategy-the-golden-image-brid.core: Don't rewrite everything at once. Use existing CM code as the bridge: run your Puppet, Chef or Ansible code inside Packer to bake golden images, so the logic is reused while deployment becomes immutable. Then migrate workload by workload (stateless first, stateful last), shrink what CM does at runtime, and finally retire the CM servers once no fleet depends on runtime convergence.

first_principles.problem: A big-bang rewrite from Chef to containers stalls after a year with nothing shipped.
truths: Existing code encodes years of knowledge.

analogy.title: Moving house room by room
analogy.story: Pack and move one room at a time, using your existing boxes, rather than demolishing and rebuilding overnight.
analogy.breaks: Rooms are independent; services have dependencies to sequence.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Same Chef role, now baked; no Chef server at runtime.

check.q: Why bake existing CM code into images rather than rewriting first?
check.a: It reuses years of proven configuration logic while immediately gaining immutable deployment, delivering value incrementally.
